questions.question: What is the 4/5ths rule (disparate impact ratio) used for?
choices: Measuring the total number of approved vs denied outputs
Comparing approval rates between demographic groups to detect bias
Counting how many times each group appears in the dataset
Calculating the average response time of the AI model
questions.explanation: The 4/5ths rule compares approval RATES between groups. If one group's rate is less than 80% of another group's rate, bias is flagged. It uses rates, not raw counts.

questions.question: Why is comparing raw counts (instead of rates) a critical mistake in bias detection?
choices: Raw counts are slower to compute than rates
A larger group will naturally have more approvals even with the same rate, masking bias
Raw counts don't include demographic information
Counts are less precise than percentages
questions.explanation: If Group A has 1,000 people and Group B has 10, comparing raw counts will always make Group B look 'underrepresented' — even if both groups have the same approval rate. Rates normalize for group size.

questions.question: Group A: 9 approved out of 10 (90%). Group B: 1 approved out of 2 (50%). What is the disparate impact ratio?
questions.explanation: The disparate impact ratio = min(rate) / max(rate) = 0.5 / 0.9 = 0.555. Since 0.555 < 0.8, this is flagged as biased. The key insight: despite Group A having 9x more approvals in raw count, the RATES reveal the real disparity.
